summary: The Dominican Republic admits tourists from the US, Canada, the UK, the EU and most of the Americas visa-free for 30 days (extendable online up to 120), requires every traveller to complete the free digital e-Ticket form for both arrival and departure, and waives its visa entirely for anyone holding a valid US, Canadian, UK or Schengen visa or residence permit.

passportValidity.text: For tourists, the Dominican Republic requires your passport to be valid for the duration of your stay — there is no formal 6-month rule, though airlines sometimes apply stricter checks of their own.

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not an entry requirement, but medical cover is strongly recommended — private clinics in tourist areas demand payment or proof of insurance before treatment, and bills can be high.

onwardTicket.text: Not always checked, but immigration rules require tourists to be able to show onward or return travel, and airlines may ask before boarding — carry a booking that leaves the country.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is set, but officers may ask about your means of support and where you will stay when granting entry.

declarations.name: e-Ticket (digital entry and exit form)
declarations.submitWindow: Complete online before departure — one form for arrival and another for departure; the QR code is checked at check-in and at the border
declarations.text: Every traveller entering or leaving the Dominican Republic by air must complete the free digital e-Ticket (a combined migration, customs and health form) and present its QR code. It is free of charge — use only the official eticket.migracion.gob.do site, as unofficial lookalike sites charge for it.

source.name: e-Ticket — official portal, Dirección General de Migración

currencyLimits.text: Cash and monetary instruments over USD 10,000 (or equivalent) must be declared on arrival and departure — the declaration is part of the e-Ticket form.

source.name: Dirección General de Aduanas — Dominican customs

notes: Duty-free allowance: 200 cigarettes, up to 2 litres of alcohol and gifts up to about USD 500 per adult (once every 3 months).
Fresh fruit, plants and animal products are restricted — declare them on the e-Ticket or leave them at home.

payments.text: Cards are accepted at resorts, hotels, malls and larger restaurants, and US dollars are widely taken in tourist zones. Carry pesos in cash for local restaurants, small shops, guaguas (local buses) and rural areas — and prefer ATMs inside banks or resorts.

safety.text: Resort areas such as Punta Cana are heavily policed (CESTUR tourist police) and generally safe; petty theft, bag-snatching from motorbikes and occasional armed robbery are risks in cities, especially after dark. Keep valuables out of sight, use trusted transport, and stick to well-lit areas at night.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Dominican Republic Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to April brings dry, sunny weather and the least humidity — peak beach season. Hurricane season officially runs June–November, with the highest storm risk August–October.

tips.text: The e-Ticket entry/exit form is free at eticket.migracion.gob.do — lookalike websites charge for the same form. Fill in one for arrival and one for departure and save the QR codes on your phone.

All-inclusive resorts are only one side of the country — Santo Domingo's Zona Colonial (the oldest European city in the Americas), Samaná's whales (January–March) and Cabarete's kitesurfing are easy add-ons; use pesos and expect a different price level outside resorts.

Motoconchos (moto-taxis) are cheap but the most dangerous way to get around — helmets are rare and traffic is chaotic. Road accidents are a leading cause of tourist injury; prefer registered taxis or ride-hailing apps.
Hurricane season peaks August–October. Travel is usually fine, but buy insurance that covers weather disruption and follow local guidance if a storm approaches.

faq.question: What is the Dominican Republic e-Ticket and who needs it?
faq.answer: The e-Ticket is a free mandatory digital form combining migration, customs and health declarations. Every air traveller must complete one before arriving AND another before departing, at the official site eticket.migracion.gob.do, and show the QR code at check-in and the border. It is completely free — avoid third-party sites that charge.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for the Dominican Republic?
faq.answer: No. US citizens enter visa-free as tourists for 30 days, and the old USD 10 tourist card is now included in airline tickets. You just need a valid passport and the free e-Ticket form. Stays can be extended online up to 120 days.

faq.question: Can I stay longer than 30 days in the Dominican Republic?
faq.answer: Yes. You can request an extension online from the Dirección General de Migración for up to 120 days in total. Many visitors instead simply pay the overstay surcharge at the airport when leaving — it is a sliding fee that grows with the overstay — but the formal extension is the correct route.

faq.question: Do I still need to buy a tourist card for the Dominican Republic?
faq.answer: No. The USD 10 tourist card was rolled into airline ticket taxes years ago, so travellers arriving by air no longer buy one separately. Nothing needs to be paid on arrival — only the free e-Ticket form is required.

faq.question: Can I enter the Dominican Republic with a US, UK or Schengen visa instead of a Dominican visa?
faq.answer: Yes. Nationals of visa-required countries (such as China, India, the Philippines or Vietnam) can enter the Dominican Republic visa-free as tourists if they hold a valid visa or residence permit for the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom or the Schengen area. They complete the normal e-Ticket and enter under the tourist regime.
